Internalizing the Future: A Unified Agentic Training Paradigm for World Model Planning

Xuan Zhang1,2,3    Zhijian Zhou1,2,3    Lingfeng Qiao3    Yulei Qin3    Ke Li3    Xing Sun3    Xiaoyu Tan3†    Chao Qu1†    Yuan Qi1† Affiliation: 1Fudan University, 2Shanghai Innovation Institute, 3Tencent Youtu Lab
June 25, 2026
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capability in sequential decision-making, yet they remains fundamentally reactive in long-horizon tasks. Unlike humans who employ ”what-if” reasoning to evaluate potential plans before commitment, standard agents lack an internal world model to simulate future outcomes. Therefore, we propose to internalize future-aware planning by training a single autoregressive model to verbalize both a prospective state rollout and a plan-conditioned success estimate—a textual analogue of the QQ-value. Crucially, we identify a format-capability gap: simply fine-tuning agents on look-ahead traces during post-training leads to superficial mimicry of foresight without genuine predictive grounding. To bridge this gap, we introduce a three-stage training paradigm: (i) World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT) to inject latent predictive capabilities into the policy; (ii) Format-Eliciting SFT (FE-SFT) to structure this injected capability; and (iii) Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (FC-RL) to refine the calibration and utility of the generated simulations. Evaluated on search and mathematical reasoning tasks, our approach consistently outperforms other training baselines. Our results demonstrate that effective internal world modeling in LLM agents requires a capability-first training pipeline to achieve grounded and calibrated foresight.

1 Introduction

LLM agents have become strong controllers for multi-step tasks given their comprehensive pre-trained semantic knowledge and remarkable capabilities in sequential decision-making [45, 42]. However, the prevailing paradigm in long-horizon settings remains fundamentally reactive, yet human planning is rarely reactive. Before acting, people often ask a what-if question: if I follow this plan, what is likely to happen next, and how likely is it to succeed? This style of reasoning is central to intelligent behavior because it allows alternatives to be mentally compared before commitment, as shown in Figure 1. In Craik’s classic formulation, effective intelligence depends on carrying a “small-scale model” of external reality that lets possible actions be tried out in thought before they are executed [5]. Inspired by this pattern of planning, we do not claim full counterfactual reasoning; rather, we target a plan-conditioned form of future simulation and evaluation within a language agent.

While standard autoregressive reasoning methods such as Chain-of-Thought [48] mainly improve decomposition of the current problem, the ability that we aim to inject is closely related to an internal world model [43, 16]. Instead of utilizing separate modules to serve as external world models [3, 47, 15], our key claim is that, for language agents, this kind of future-aware planning signal should be internalized as part of the policy itself. Moreover, unlike Dreamer-style model-based RL [17, 18, 19], our goal is not to introduce a separate simulator or a dedicated value head. Instead, we train a single autoregressive model not only to serve as a reasoning agent, but also to verbalize both: (i) a compact prospective rollout of what may happen next, and (ii) a plan-conditioned estimate of success if the current plan is followed. This textual estimate is best understood as a verbalized analogue of Q⁡(s,a)Q(s,a) or local action value, represented in the same token space as the policy rather than as a claim of full what-if reasoning. Unlike other methods that only train agents to predict future states or transition dynamics [4, 8, 52], our design of internal world modeling is more comprehensive and innovative. Crucially, our verbalized QQ-values are designed to be continuously updated and corrected by actual environmental feedback obtained from real execution during RL training, which is also distinct from previous works [20].

Such explicit verbalization offers a transparent reasoning signal, allowing the agent to effectively prune suboptimal paths through implicit deliberation. To inject this capability, a natural idea is to leverage the inherent world modeling potential of LLMs [28] by training the agent to imagine the future, evaluate it, and then act. However, our preliminary experiments show that this strategy fails when applied only during post-training. With SFT and RL on formatted look-ahead traces, the agent learns the surface form of a simulation but not the predictive competence behind it. Experimental results for SFT and RL are shown in Table 7, and an example is shown in Appendix E.1. We call this failure mode the format-capability gap: the agent can produce a plausible-looking foresight block while the content remains weakly grounded, miscalibrated, or outright misleading, thus introducing noise rather than useful guidance.

This motivates us to propose a unified three-stage training paradigm: World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT), Format-Eliciting SFT (FE-SFT), and Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (FC-RL). WM-AMT injects the underlying predict-then-act capability by augmenting large-scale agentic trajectories with future-aware experience summaries. FE-SFT then teaches the model when and how to externalize this latent capability in a structured foresight block. FC-RL finally improves both action quality and foresight quality by rewarding task success, grounded anticipation, and calibrated confidence. All three stages are implemented within one causal language model, with no additional value head.

We evaluate this training paradigm on two representative agentic domains: search and mathematical reasoning. Across both settings, our method consistently outperforms other training baselines. The results show that future-aware behavior in LLM agents is not well served by format supervision alone; it benefits from a training pipeline that first builds the capability, then elicits it, and finally optimizes it under reward.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify the format-capability gap: post-training on look-ahead formats alone teaches LLM agents to mimic the structure of foresight without reliably acquiring grounded future prediction.

  • •

    We propose a unified three-stage paradigm, consisting of WM-AMT, FE-SFT, and FC-RL, which internalizes world-model planning inside a single autoregressive policy. Our method verbalizes both future rollout and a plan-conditioned success estimate without introducing an explicit value head, and this verbalized Q-like signal is explicitly trained and refined throughout the pipeline.

  • •

    We show on search and mathematical reasoning that this capability-first pipeline yields consistent gains over other training baselines.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 World models in LLM agents

We formulate LLM agents’ decision-making as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) [2], denoted by ℳ=⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,ℛ,γ⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle. State st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} includes the initial instruction, historical trajectory, and observations. Action at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} represents discrete operations, e.g., text generation or tool invocation. Transition dynamics 𝒫⁡(st+1|st,at)\mathcal{P}(s_{t+1}|s_{t},a_{t}) and reward ℛ⁡(st,at)\mathcal{R}(s_{t},a_{t}) govern environmental feedback. The objective is to learn a parameterized policy πθ​(at|st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t}) that maximizes the expected return discounted by γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]. World models traditionally predict transition dynamics 𝒫^​(st+1|st,at)\hat{\mathcal{P}}(s_{t+1}|s_{t},a_{t}) and rewards ℛ^​(st,at)\hat{\mathcal{R}}(s_{t},a_{t}) [43]. However, applying token-level simulation to dense, low-level environmental feedback is computationally intractable. Autoregressively predicting fine-grained future trajectories τf​u​t​u​r​e=⟨st+1,at+1,ot+1,…,st+k⟩\tau_{future}=\langle s_{t+1},a_{t+1},o_{t+1},\dots,s_{t+k}\rangle may waste computational capacity on syntax rather than core causal dynamics, thus causing severe compounding errors [27]. Thus, we reconceptualize the World Model for LLM agents as an internal semantic simulator. It generates a condensed experience summary of anticipated consequences, defined as z^t=Ψ⁡(τf​u​t​u​r​e)\hat{z}_{t}=\Psi(\tau_{future}). Here, Ψ\Psi is a semantic compression function mapping raw rollouts into high-level predictive foresight. This empowers the agent to perform look-ahead planning, transitioning from a reactive policy πθ​(at|st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t}) to a foresight-conditioned policy πθ​(at|st,z^t)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t},\hat{z}_{t}). Ultimately, this enables the agent to evaluate consequences and prune suboptimal trajectories in the latent space before executing real-world actions.

2.2 Mid-training in large language models

To obtain strong initial policies in terms of both performance and exploration diversity, mid-training [32, 41] has become an essential step between general pre-training and post-training, which aims to adapt the LLM’s underlying data distribution toward the target domain. Recent theoretical analyses demonstrate that an effective mid-training stage not only establishes strong policy priors by efficiently pruning the decision space, but also allows the subsequent RL phase to effectively jump across multiple steps during Bellman backups, thus accelerating convergence speed and minimizing post-training regret [53]. By immersing the LLM in high-density, high-quality specialized sequences, mid-training provides a latent semantic foundation and contextually grounded initialization for post-training.

2.3 Group-based RL

Unlike traditional Actor-Critic methods (e.g., PPO [38]) that rely on a parameterized value network Vϕ​(s)V_{\phi}(s) to estimate advantages, group-based RL approaches [39, 51, 11] leverage the statistical distribution of rewards within a sampled batch to approximate the baseline. For a given task prompt xx, the agent samples a group of GG trajectories {τ1,τ2,…,τG}\{\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\dots,\tau_{G}\} from the current policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}. Each trajectory τi\tau_{i} represents a full episode of interactions and is assigned a scalar reward R⁡(τi)R(\tau_{i}) reflecting the task success. The advantage estimation A⁡(τi)A(\tau_{i}) is derived from the normalized reward in each group: A⁡(τi)=R⁡(τi)−μ⁡({R⁡(τj)}j=1G)σ⁡({R⁡(τj)}j=1G)A(\tau_{i})=\frac{R(\tau_{i})-\mu(\{R(\tau_{j})\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\sigma(\{R(\tau_{j})\}_{j=1}^{G})}, where μ\mu and σ\sigma denote the mean and standard deviation of rewards in the group, respectively.

3 Methodology

3.1 The format-capability gap in post-training

A natural idea to internalize world model into the LLM policy is training the LLM with SFT data that explicitly includes anticipated futures, and then followed by RL. However, our preliminary experiments on the model mid-trained with routine agentic trajectories (see Appendix D.1 and E.1) reveal a format-capability gap. While the agent learns the format of look-ahead reasoning, it fails to simulate accurate future dynamics, often resulting in hallucinations. We attribute it to the inherent nature of post-training: while SFT and RL excel at eliciting latent capabilities, they struggle to inject fundamentally new ones. Without a prior understanding of future consequences, enforcing a look-ahead format merely triggers hallucinated pattern matching rather than genuine future simulation. It motivates us to intervene earlier in the training pipeline via mid-training to construct a foundational data distribution that intrinsically models the future. We propose a three-stage training paradigm to close the format-capability gap, as shown in Figure 2. Given an LLM policy, our goal is not only to produce a well-formed look-ahead trace, but also to internalize transition-aware foresight that improves policy capability. The paradigm consists of: (i) World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT) for policy prior formation, (ii) Format-Eliciting Supervised Fine-Tuning (FE-SFT) for structured elicitation, and (iii) Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (FC-RL) for reward-aligned policy optimization.

3.2 World model agentic mid-training

Standard pre-training and agentic SFT trajectory data primarily consist of observational trajectories. While this paradigm trains the model to predict the next action given the historical context, we aim to instill look-ahead capabilities in LLM agents via WM-AMT (Algorithm 1). Let 𝒟raw={τi}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\text{raw}}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote a large-scale dataset of agentic trajectories, where each trajectory is defined as a sequence of state-action pairs: τ=(s1,a1,s2,a2,…,sT,aT)\tau=(s_{1},a_{1},s_{2},a_{2},\dots,s_{T},a_{T}). Instead of relying on human-annotated chain-of-thought data, we systematically augment 𝒟raw\mathcal{D}_{\text{raw}} through a trajectory summarization mapping.

Formally, for a given trajectory τ\tau of length TT, we sample a set of indices ℐ∼𝒰⁡(1,T−1)\mathcal{I}\sim\mathcal{U}(1,T-1). For each step t∈ℐt\in\mathcal{I}, we construct a structured world model block ztz_{t}. We define a summarization function Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot), which maps the current observation sts_{t} and the future trajectory τ>t\tau_{>t} into a composite textual representation: zt=[zt(traj)⊕zt(eval)]z_{t}=[z_{t}^{(\text{traj})}\oplus z_{t}^{(\text{eval})}]. Here, zt(traj)z_{t}^{(\text{traj})} serves as an abstracted roadmap of the simulated future. zt(eval)z_{t}^{(\text{eval})} provides a semantic gap analysis and a QQ-value estimation q∈[0,100]%q\in[0,100]\%, denoting the confidence score of successfully resolving the initial task following this roadmap. While accurately estimating qq for merely a single step of a trajectory ideally requires dozens of Monte Carlo rollouts, it is computationally prohibitive given the massive scale of mid-training data. Consequently, we adopt an LLM to heuristically estimate this success probability. Though this estimation may be not accurate enough, it is acceptable because these confidence priors are ultimately grounded and calibrated against true execution outcomes during subsequent RL training.

We then inject ztz_{t} into the original agentic trajectory, producing an augmented trajectory τ~\tilde{\tau}, which is defined by τ~=(…,st,zt,at,st+1,…)\tilde{\tau}=(\dots,s_{t},z_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1},\dots). The WM-AMT stage optimizes the policy θ\theta via the standard autoregressive negative log-likelihood objective over the augmented dataset 𝒟WM-AMT\mathcal{D}_{\text{WM-AMT}}: ℒWM-AMT​(θ)=−𝔼τ~∼𝒟WM-AMT​[∑i=1|τ~|log⁡Pθ​(ui|u<i)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{WM-AMT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{\tau}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{WM-AMT}}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{|\tilde{\tau}|}\log P_{\theta}(u_{i}|u_{<i})\right], where uiu_{i} denotes the ii-th token in τ~\tilde{\tau}. By forcing the model to autoregressively reconstruct the composite block ztz_{t} conditioned strictly on the history up to sts_{t}, the objective functions as an implicit world model, equipping the agent with both causal prediction and value evaluation capabilities.

3.3 Format-eliciting supervised fine-tuning

While WM-AMT successfully injects latent look-ahead capabilities into LLM agents, the base policy lacks the structural schema to autonomously and reliably invoke this predictive capability during inference. The FE-SFT stage bridges this gap by aligning the generated trajectory with a predefined, explicit look-ahead reasoning structure. We curate a filtered task-specific instruction-tuning dataset 𝒟FE-SFT\mathcal{D}_{\text{FE-SFT}}. Given a current observation sts_{t}, the policy is trained to project its internal world model into a textual representation of anticipated future states and estimated QQ-values, i.e., world model block z^t\hat{z}_{t}. While adopting a similar generation pipeline for these instances, FE-SFT strictly encloses z^t\hat{z}_{t} within distinct structural delimiters. Following z^t\hat{z}_{t}, the policy generates the corresponding executable action ata_{t}. Since WM-AMT has established a robust causal prior via a large-scale general agentic trajectories, FE-SFT avoids the hallucinations typical of world modeling from scratch. We also use the standard autoregressive negative log-likelihood objective to optimize the agent on 𝒟FE-SFT\mathcal{D}_{\text{FE-SFT}}.

3.4 Foresight-conditioned RL

The policy may still suffer from compounding errors during long-horizon inference or produce miscalibrated foresight after WM-AMT and FE-SFT. To jointly optimize the internalized world model and the policy, we introduce FC-RL (Algorithm 2). The agent serves as two roles and generates a structured trajectory in an interaction loop: imaginary→keyword→analysis→confidence​(qt)⏟World Model Span ​(𝒯WM)→think→action​(at)⏟Policy Span ​(𝒯Policy)\underbrace{\textit{imaginary}\rightarrow\textit{keyword}\rightarrow\textit{analysis}\rightarrow\textit{confidence}\ (q_{t})}_{\text{World Model Span }(\mathcal{T}_{\text{WM}})}\rightarrow\underbrace{\textit{think}\rightarrow\textit{action}\ (a_{t})}_{\text{Policy Span }(\mathcal{T}_{\text{Policy}})}.

To jointly optimize final task success and intermediate foresight quality, we decompose the training objective into world model optimization and policy optimization. For a given prompt, we sample a group of NN trajectories {τ1,…,τN}\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{N}\}.

World model optimization: foresight grounding and calibration

To ensure the internal world model provides reliable planning rather than hallucinations, we optimize it from two complementary dimensions: causal accuracy and value calibration.

First, to penalize hallucinated simulations, we introduce a grounding reward RgroundR_{\text{ground}}. The agent abstracts its look-ahead trajectory into milestones, denoted as keywords KtK_{t}. We define Rgroundi,t=Rmatch​(Kt(i),τ>t(i))R_{\text{ground}}^{i,t}=R_{\text{match}}(K_{t}^{(i)},\tau_{>t}^{(i)}), a verification function that rewards the model only if its predicted keywords successfully manifest in the actual execution.

Second, to ensure the accuracy of the agent’s internal QQ-value estimation and explicitly penalize miscalibrated foresight, we apply a Brier score penalty [13] to the confidence qt(i)q_{t}^{(i)}. Upon episode completion, the environment provides a terminal correctness evaluation, yielding a binary outcome indicator 𝐈\mathbf{I}, i.e., 𝐈y≡y∗\mathbf{I}_{y\equiv y^{*}}, where yy is the predicted answer and y∗y^{*} is the ground truth. From a Monte Carlo (MC) perspective, 𝐈\mathbf{I} serves as an unbiased, single-sample empirical return for the trajectory from step tt. To calibrate qtq_{t}, we treat this MC return as the ground truth and apply a Brier score-based calibration reward:

Rcalibi,t=Rcalib​(yi,qt(i),yi∗)=𝐈−(qt(i)−𝐈)2R_{\text{calib}}^{i,t}=R_{\text{calib}}(y_{i},q_{t}^{(i)},y_{i}^{*})=\mathbf{I}-(q_{t}^{(i)}-\mathbf{I})^{2} (1)

By utilizing the terminal correctness to calibrate the intermediate qtq_{t}, it forces the agent to align its self-assessed QQ-values, i.e., confidence on future, with the empirical success rate.

Finally, we compute a combined step-level world model reward RWM​(τit)=Rcalibi,t+Rgroundi,tR^{\text{WM}}(\tau_{i}^{t})=R_{\text{calib}}^{i,t}+R_{\text{ground}}^{i,t}. We obtain the final world model advantage A⁡(τ​[world_model]it)A(\tau[\text{world\_model}]_{i}^{t}) by normalizing these combined rewards across all the corresponding steps {RWM​(τit)}i=1N\{R^{\text{WM}}(\tau_{i}^{t})\}_{i=1}^{N} within the group.

Policy optimization: execution success

For long-horizon tasks, relying solely on the terminal global advantage may suffer from sparse and delayed credit assignment, so we introduce a local (step) reward RS​(τit)=qt(i)R^{S}(\tau_{i}^{t})=q_{t}^{(i)}. Let AE​(τi)A^{E}(\tau_{i}) denote the global advantage computed by normalizing the episode rewards RiER^{E}_{i} across the group. Similarly, let AS​(τit)A^{S}(\tau_{i}^{t}) represent the step-level advantage, normalized across all the confidence of corresponding steps {qt(i)}i=1N\{q_{t}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} within the group. The final combined advantage for the policy is defined as:

A⁡(τ​[policy]it)=AE​(τi)+ω⋅AS​(τit)A(\tau[\text{policy}]_{i}^{t})=A^{E}(\tau_{i})+\omega\cdot A^{S}(\tau_{i}^{t}) (2)

where ω\omega balances global task success and local foresight alignment. Crucially, since qt(i)q_{t}^{(i)} is explicitly calibrated via world model optimization, it mitigates the risk of reward hacking and serves as a reliable proxy for the policy. The policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} is then updated by maximizing the clipped GRPO surrogate objective utilizing the advantage A⁡(τ​[policy]it)A(\tau[\text{policy}]_{i}^{t}).

4 Related Work

4.1 World models in autonomous agents

World models are core to model-based RL, where agents learn transition and reward for look-ahead control [43, 33]. Classical lines focus on latent-dynamics learning in visually observed environments [16, 17, 18, 19] and more recently, embodied agent for future action-conditioned simulation [12]. It enables models to improve sample efficiency in a latent space or simulate outcomes without real-world interaction. The idea has shifted from pixel-space simulation to language-mediated future prediction and planning due to the rise of LLMs [20, 3]; it also extends to code-generation settings, where world modeling is used to study long-horizon program synthesis and repair [8]. Despite these advancements, most existing systems treat the world model as an explicit simulator or external module [47, 15]. For example, WebDreamer [15] and WebEvolver [9] construct explicit world models to simulate the environmental feedback, which improve deliberation quality but may introduce additional inference overhead and possible simulator-policy mismatch. In parallel, recent implicit world modeling strategies suggest that early experiences can improve downstream agent behavior without relying on another simulator [4, 52]. Extending this implicit world modeling line, our work targets a unified agentic training pipeline for world model planning.

4.2 Agentic data synthesis and mid-training

The scarcity of expert-level demonstrations has motivated the synthetic data for training LLM agents [52]. Early imitation-based distillation from stronger teachers [34, 7] aids initial alignment but suffers from limited diversity and weak on-policy coverage. Subsequent works, such as AgentSynth [49] and SCA [54], broaden task synthesis to expand the exploration space for agentic RL. Another direction shifts from trajectory synthesis to environment synthesis, e.g., classical world-model methods in Section 4.1, which uses learned environments to generate scalable interaction data. However, translating these synthetic interactions into reusable decision-making capabilities necessitates a dedicated training phase. Consequently, mid-training [32] is increasingly adopted to bridge general pre-training and task-level alignment [41, 53]. Unlike SFT, mid-training scales to vastly larger, diverse corpora of expert rollouts, such as human demonstrations in device control, tool-use records and code writing [37, 22, 1]. Our perspective is to synthesize agentic data with compressed future experience summary, and internalize a robust predict-then-act policy prior via mid-training.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experiment setup

We select an intermediate checkpoint of Youtu-LLM-2B [29] as our foundation model, and refer to it as Youtu-LLM-2B-Init. This selection is motivated by two practical considerations: (1) the Youtu-LLM family inherently possesses strong native agentic capabilities; (2) a lightweight 2B scale makes our extensive mid-training computationally feasible. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we initialize from the Youtu-LLM-2B-Init immediately following its general pre-training and compare two mid-training variants: (1) Youtu-LLM-2B-Base is trained with standard agentic mid-training on 200B tokens of high-quality agentic trajectory data without changing its structure; (2) Youtu-LLM-2B-Base (WM-AMT, ours) augments the same agentic trajectory data by inserting an explicit world model block into a random split of multi-turn interaction trajectories, which provides supervised signals for future-state prediction. We conduct experiments on two representative agentic tasks: search and mathematical reasoning.

Search

Following Jin et al. [23], we evaluate our training paradigm on 7 search-augmented QA tasks, including single-hop QA datasets (NQ [26], TriviaQA [24], and PopQA [31]) and multi-hop QA datasets (HotpotQA [50], 2Wiki [21], MuSiQue [44], and Bamboogle [35]). For retrieval, we use the 2018 Wikipedia dump [25] as the knowledge source and E5 [46] as the retriever, and set the number of retrieved passages to 3 across all retrieval-based methods. During evaluation, the results are obtained via greedy sampling, and the metrics are computed via LLM-as-a-judge using DeepSeek V3.1 [6].

Mathematical reasoning

Following Feng et al. [10], we evaluate our paradigm on AIME2024/2025/2026 [30]. We repeat the evaluation set AIME2024&2025&2026 30 times and report both mean@3030 and pass@3030. The evaluation hyperparameters of evaluation are set to temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.6.

Baselines and configurations

(1) Post-Training Only*: Our preliminary experiments are conducted directly on Youtu-LLM-2B-Base, serving as a vanilla baseline that only applies post-training without any world-model-augmented mid-training. (2) State-Only Prediction (Post-Training Only)†\dagger: The agent is trained only via post-training to predict future states but omits the verbalized QQ-values. This setup mirrors other methods of predicting only state transitions [4]. (3) State-Only Prediction (With Mid-Training)‡\ddagger: The agent is trained via mid-training and post-training to predict future states but omits the verbalized QQ-values. This setup mirrors other methods introducing large-scale mid-training for world modeling [8]. (4) IWM: We apply the core world-modeling data generation pipeline of [52] to our task. Detailed training hyperparameters are presented in Appendix C.3.3.

5.2 Main results

Necessity of our three phases.

(1) WM-AMT: At the SFT stage, replacing standard agentic mid-training with our WM-AMT improves the average score under the same SFT method (e.g., in Table 1, 38.2 →\rightarrow 39.9 for SFT and 37.4 →\rightarrow 41.8 for FE-SFT). We provide a case study in Appendix E.1: under the same FE-SFT format, our WM-AMT model generates more coherent, causally accurate world model blocks, while the base model fails. These results indicate that FE-SFT is substantially effective when the model has internalized future-dynamics priors via WM-AMT. (2) FE-SFT: Under our WM-AMT model, our FE-SFT outperforms standard SFT (e.g. 39.9 →\rightarrow 41.8 in Table 1), showing that explicitly eliciting structured foresight is beneficial after the world-model capability is established. (3) FC-RL: In RL-stage comparisons, our FE-SFT & FC-RL achieves the best overall average (50.6 in Table 1, mean@30: 29.5 and pass@30: 60.0 in Table 2), outperforming all the other baselines.

Stage dependency.

The overall results exhibit a progressive dependency: WM-AMT provides a capability foundation, FE-SFT activates this capability in a structured format, and FC-RL optimizes end-task behavior with grounded foresight. Removing or replacing any stage weakens the final performance, confirming the need for the full pipeline.

Comparison with other world modeling methods.

In Table 1, the highest average score of state-only baselines is 48.7; while in Table 2, it achieves a pass@30 of 56.7 and a mean@30 of 27.7. By adding the verbalized QQ-value and applying our FC-RL to jointly optimize the policy and its internalized world model, our final model (WM-AMT & FE-SFT & FC-RL) increases these scores to 50.6 in Table 1, 60.0 (pass@30) and 29.5 (mean@30) in Table 2, respectively. It proves that simply predicting future states is not enough for world modeling. Instead, explicitly adding the confidence estimation and utilizing the calibrated confidence to guide the policy are crucial for making better decisions. Notably, IWM (+RL) achieves strong performance on Youtu-LLM-2B-Base, but our final model still shows a significant and consistent improvement.

Efficacy on complex multi-hop reasoning.

Another notable fact is that our proposed paradigm yields particularly pronounced improvements on complex, multi-step reasoning tasks in Table 1. Up to the SFT stage, the transition from SFT to FE-SFT under our WM-AMT model brings a significant improvement (MuSiQue: 20.6 →\rightarrow 25.6, 2WikiMultiHopQA: 31.2 →\rightarrow 35.8). Our final model also demonstrates substantial superiority on multi-hop datasets compared to the other baselines, e.g., HotpotQA (59.0), MuSiQue (34.2) and Bamboogle (56.0). It indicates that the internalized world model and foresight-conditioned planning are especially critical for tasks requiring long-horizon reasoning, whereas simple factual retrieval (single-hop) relies less heavily on future simulation.

Qualitative analysis of world model blocks.

We provide examples in Appendix E.2 and E.3 to analyze the world model blocks. Two key capabilities emerge: (1) Long-horizon planning coherence: these blocks establish reasoning frameworks that persist across multiple turns, even when intermediate errors require correction; and (2) Calibrated confidence quantification: confidence estimates correlate meaningfully with the actual task success, decreasing upon error detection and remaining low for inherently challenging problems.

Additional ablation studies, sensitivity analyses on ω\omega in FC-RL, and analyses on the response length are provided in Appendix D.2, D.3 and D.4.

6 Conclusion

We address the limitations of reactive LLM agents by internalizing future-aware planning into the policy. We identify the format-capability gap, wherein post-training on look-ahead formats merely teaches structural mimicry instead of grounded prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose a unified three-stage training paradigm consisting of WM-AMT, FE-SFT and FC-RL. Evaluations across search and mathematical reasoning show the superiority of our approach over other training baselines. Our results underscore that effective internal world modeling in LLM agents demands a capability-first paradigm to achieve truly grounded and calibrated foresight.

Appendix B Data construction

B.1 World model agentic mid-training

To construct the structured world model Block ztz_{t} during the World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT) phase, we employ an LLM acting as the summarization function Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot). The prompt enforces abstract planning to prevent future-state data leakage and explicitly requires confidence estimation for QQ-value modeling. The exact prompt template is provided below:

We leverage DeepSeek V3.1 [6] as the foundational data generator for World Model Agentic Mid-Training. The model is queried using the above prompt, with generation parameters set to a temperature of 0.6, a top-p of 0.95, and a maximum response length of 32768 tokens.

The original agentic trajectory data consists of 200B tokens of high-quality trajectory data, including 25B Agentic-CoT trajectories, 20B mathematical trajectories, 70B code execution trajectories, 60B Deep Research trajectories, and 25B other trajectories (e.g., tool using, function calling, and planning).

In WM-AMT, we augment the original agentic trajectory data by inserting an explicit world model block into a random split of multi-turn interaction trajectories, which are primarily concentrated in Deep Research trajectories and mathematical trajectories. After our data augmentation, we obtained roughly ∼62\sim 62B tokens for Deep Research trajectories and ∼21\sim 21B for mathematics, whereas the remaining trajectory categories remained unaltered.

B.2 Format-eliciting supervised fine-tuning

The prompt and generation configurations for foresight block construction in FE-SFT is as the same as the prompt in WM-AMT, with only additional formatting applied. Particularly, the seperate prompt for extracting keywords from the foresight block is as follows:

We also leverage DeepSeek V3.1 for extracting keywords, with generation parameters set to a temperature of 0.6, a top-p of 0.95, and a maximum response length of 4096 tokens.

We constructed ∼4​k\sim 4k trajectories for the search task, reformulated into ∼13​k\sim 13k single-turn samples to align with the verl-agent framework for SFT. For the mathematical reasoning task, we curated ∼2​k\sim 2k trajectories specifically for SFT.

C.3.2 Outcome reward function

Search

We adopt an LLM-as-a-judge outcome reward as follows:

R⁡(a,a^)={1,if exact_match​(a,a^)LLM_judge​(a,a^),otherwise\small R(a,\hat{a})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if exact\_match}(a,\hat{a})\\ \text{LLM\_judge}(a,\hat{a}),&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

where aa and a^\hat{a} represent the ground-truth answer and the predicted answer, respectively. A reward of 1 is assigned directly for an Exact Match (EM), while in other cases, an LLM-as-a-judge (DeepSeek-V3.1 in our experiments) is employed to evaluate the response and determine the reward, such that LLM_judge​(a,a^)∈{0,1}\text{LLM\_judge}(a,\hat{a})\in\{0,1\}.

The prompt for LLM-as-a-judge is as follows:

The generation parameters are set to a temperature of 0.6, a top-p of 0.95, and a maximum response length of 1024 tokens.

Particularly, invalid actions are penalized with a reward of -0.01.

Mathematical reasoning

We adopt a composite outcome reward function that evaluates both the final answer correctness and the agent’s intermediate tool utilization. We require the model to present final answers in a specified format (e.g., within \boxed{}), enabling reliable rule-based correctness verification. The reward is formulated as:

Rbase​(a,a^)={1,is_equivalent​(a,a^)−1,otherwiseR_{\text{base}}(a,\hat{a})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{is\_equivalent}(a,\hat{a})\\ -1,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

where aa and a^\hat{a} represent the ground-truth answer and the predicted answer, respectively.

To encourage the model to engage in multi-turn reasoning and actively call tools, we also introduce a tool utilization reward, denoted as RtoolR_{\text{tool}}, which scales linearly with the number of conversation turns NN:

Rtool=0.05×(N−2)R_{\text{tool}}=0.05\times(N-2)

The final reward SfinalS_{\text{final}} integrates the base score and the tool reward through a conditional aggregation strategy to prevent reward hacking:

Sfinal={min⁡(0,Sbase+Rtool),if ​Sbase<0Sbase+𝕀⁡(N>2),otherwiseS_{\text{final}}=\begin{cases}\min(0,S_{\text{base}}+R_{\text{tool}}),&\text{if }S_{\text{base}}<0\\ S_{\text{base}}+\mathbb{I}(N>2),&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

where 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) is an indicator function that yields 11 if the condition is met and 00 otherwise.

Appendix D Additional experimental results

D.1 The format-capability gap in post-training

The results for post-training on Youtu-LLM-2B-Base mid-trained with routine agentic trajectories (preliminary experiments mentioned in Section 5.1) are shown in Table 7. As the tables show, directly applying post-training methods on the standard base model (Youtu-LLM-2B-Base) does not yield significant improvements. This indicates that post-training alone is not enough to teach the model how to plan and reason accordingly.

To ensure that the format-capability gap is a general phenomenon rather than an artifact of the particular model, we conducted parallel preliminary experiments on two other distinct models: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct [14] and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [36]. The results shown in Table 8 consistently reproduced our initial observation, confirming that direct post-training on these standard models similarly fails to elicit genuine planning capabilities. However, due to the prohibitive computational resources required for the extensive mid-training phase, coupled with the practical constraint that intermediate, pre-mid-training checkpoints for these model families are publicly unavailable to establish a controlled baseline, we do not execute the full mid-training process on these architectures for the subsequent stages.

The model trained solely via SFT and RL on reasoning-enhanced data may achieve high ”format accuracy” but low ”semantic accuracy”. The predicted futures possibly diverge from the ground truth or hallucinate non-existent state transitions, as examples in Appendix E.1 show. Instead of providing useful guidance, these inaccurate predictions introduce noise into the reasoning process, leading to suboptimal policy performance.

D.2 Sensitivity analysis on ω\omega

Table 9 shows the results of our experiments with different values of ω\omega, which balances the policy objective in our FC-RL, for the search task.

We observe that the performance initially improves as ω\omega increases, reaching an optimal average score of 50.6 at ω=0.2\omega=0.2. This represents a 1.5% absolute improvement over the baseline (ω=0\omega=0), particularly excelling in multi-hop tasks like HotpotQA. However, a further increase to ω=0.5\omega=0.5 leads to a performance drop (but comparable to the baseline), suggesting that an excessively high ww is not advisable since it may distract the agent from fundamental reasoning capabilities.

D.3 Ablation studies on RgroundR_{\text{ground}} in FC-RL

We conduct ablation studies on RgroundR_{\text{ground}} in FC-RL for the search task, and the results are presented in Table 10.

The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the grounding reward RgroundR_{\text{ground}} in enhancing the agent’s factuality and reasoning stability. By incorporating RgroundR_{\text{ground}}, we observe that the average score increases from 50.1 to 50.6, where the model benefits significantly from the fine-grained guidance provided by the grounding reward to align its outputs with retrieved evidence.

D.4 Analysis of response length

To evaluate whether the internalized world model introduces excessive inference overhead, we compare the average response length (total number of tokens per agentic trajectory) of our FE-SFT model against a standard SFT baseline.

The results in Table 11 show that the inclusion of explicit world model blocks leads to only a marginal increase in response length (under 19% across both tasks). This minimal expansion indicates that the model learns to generate highly distilled future simulations rather than verbose reasoning traces. Therefore, our paradigm enhances the agent’s foresight capabilities while maintaining an inference efficiency comparable to standard reactive policies.

D.5 Analysis of the RL-only baseline and the necessity of SFT

To address the concern regarding whether success-driven RL alone is sufficient, we introduce and evaluate the RL only baseline across both the standard base model and our mid-trained architecture. As summarized in Table 12, directly applying RL (GRPO) optimization without a preparatory SFT phase results in severe performance degradation in the search task.

Crucially, our results in Figure 3 reveals a severe optimization pathology during the RL-only training loop on tool-integrated search tasks. Without a preliminary SFT phase to anchor the structural tool-calling syntax and reasoning schema, the model suffers from an alignment collapse in the later stages of training. Specifically, the agent completely forgets how to interact with external search tools. Driven by the sparse success rewards, the policy prematurely converges on a degenerative local optimum: it collapses into a naive single-turn generation format, directly outputing what it speculates to be the answer while entirely bypassing the necessary multi-hop tool invocation sequences. This finding firmly demonstrates that success-driven RL alone cannot robustly bootstrap complex, structured action sequences from scratch. Consequently, a warm-start SFT phase (such as standard SFT or our proposed FE-SFT) is crucial to establish a s structural prior before exposing the agent to RL.

Appendix E Case study

E.1 An example of the format-capability gap in post-training

In the following case (A), the base model without our WM-AMT exhibits a format-capability gap in post-training, where it adopts the required output format but fails to demonstrate actual look-ahead capability. Its imaginary content is dominated by repetitive, low-information phrases such as execute a search query or search results will provide a direct answe. These statements function as generic templates rather than specific task plans and simulations. This suggests that without WM-AMT, the model merely fills a structural template with filler text without understanding the information gap between the current state and the goal. Furthermore, the base model demonstrates poor calibration in its self-assessment, assigning a ”100% confidence” score to a vague and logically inconsistent plan.

In contrast, the model enhanced by our WM-AMT moves beyond simple imitation to achieve substantive future trajectory projection in post-training. As shown in the following case (B), its content is no longer composed of empty procedural descriptions but includes highly specific task-oriented foresights. For instance, it accurately identifies the missing actor identifier and explicitly plans to extract a specific character name. Most importantly, the model demonstrates a proactive error-handling capability by anticipating potential ambiguity in search results and proposing a conditional follow-up step. Besides, the model enhanced by our WM-AMT provides a high but non-absolute confidence score (e.g., 90%), acknowledging the inherent variables in external information retrieval. This transition to a multi-step, verifiable, and calibrated reasoning process confirms that WM-AMT enables the model to effectively imagine and evaluate its future execution path in post-training.

E.2 A search example of the reasoning flow with internalized world model

The case (A) exemplifies the policy’s capacity to maintain long-horizon planning coherence. The agent’s initial imaginary block established a two-step verification protocol (identify candidate game →\rightarrow verify content characteristics), which was systematically executed across multiple search iterations spanning 6-7 information retrieval steps. Notably, the final imaginary block at Turn 7 explicitly references the verification completion, demonstrating that the strategic framework established in Turn 1 remained cognitively active and guided the reasoning process throughout the multi-step trajectory. The consistently high confidence scores (90%-95%) correlate with the eventual correct answer, indicating well-calibrated confidence estimation for successfully executed plans. Score: 1.0 (Correct).

This case (B) demonstrates a reasoning failure where the agent’s initial high-confidence prediction (95%) ultimately converges on an answer with merely 5% confidence. Critically, the extremely low confidence (5%) serves as an effective failure signal, correctly indicating that the answer lacks evidential support. The actual connection (both are Disney productions/properties) was never discovered through the search process. This case validates the hypothesis that confidence scores effectively correlate with answer correctness: the 5% confidence appropriately predicts the incorrect outcome. Score: 0.0 (Incorrect).

The two cases collectively demonstrate two key behavioral patterns of our policy with internalized world model:

  1. 1.

    Long-horizon planning coherence: In Case A, the initial imaginary block established a verification protocol that remained operationally effective across 6-7 reasoning steps. The agent systematically refined search queries while maintaining adherence to the original strategic framework, indicating that the imaginary planning mechanism successfully encodes persistent goal structures that guide subsequent policy decisions even when separated by multiple intermediate actions.

  2. 2.

    Calibrated QQ-value quantification: The confidence scores exhibit strong correlation with task success: Case A (95% confidence, correct answer), and Case B (5% confidence, incorrect answer). Notably, the confidence degradation in Cases B appropriately reflects the quality of retrieved evidence and the coherence of the reasoning trajectory, suggesting that the confidence estimation mechanism effectively reflects the QQ-value rather than merely expressing arbitrary numerical values.

E.3 A mathematical reasoning example of the reasoning flow with internalized world model

Analysis of Case (A): This example demonstrates persistent planning across multi-step reasoning. The core framework established in Turn 1 (base conversion →\rightarrow divisibility condition →\rightarrow enumeration →\rightarrow verification) persists throughout all four turns. Notably, when an algebraic error is detected in Turn 3 (confidence drops to 60%), the agent maintains its planning structure while correcting the specific erroneous component. The confidence trajectory (80%→95%→60%→99%80\%\rightarrow 95\%\rightarrow 60\%\rightarrow 99\%) reflects appropriate quantification. Score: 1.0 (Correct).

Analysis of Case (B): This example illustrates the agent’s behavior on inherently challenging problems. The confidence trajectory (20%→15%→10%→5%→⋯→15%20\%\rightarrow 15\%\rightarrow 10\%\rightarrow 5\%\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow 15\%) remains consistently low throughout the 12-turn reasoning process. Unlike Case (A), where confidence recovered after error correction, the low confidence persists here, indicating the agent’s awareness of unreliability. Score: 0.0 (Incorrect).

Analysis of Case (C): This example demonstrates declining confidence as the agent expects a lower chance of problem-solving success. The initial high confidence (90%) reflects the apparent simplicity of the combinatorial setup. However, as reasoning progresses and interpretation ambiguities emerge, confidence declines progressively (90%→95%→80%→⋯→25%90\%\rightarrow 95\%\rightarrow 80\%\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow 25\%). This pattern suggests the agent appropriately revises its QQ-value estimates in response to the lower expected success rate. Score: 0.0 (Incorrect).

These case studies presented above also provide empirical evidence for two key capabilities of our policy with internalized world model:

  1. 1.

    Long-horizon planning coherence: As demonstrated in Case (A), the high-level reasoning framework established in the initial imaginary planning block persists across multiple tool-use iterations. Notably, when intermediate errors occur (e.g., incorrect algebraic manipulation in Turn 3), the agent maintains its core planning structure while selectively revising the erroneous components, rather than abandoning the overall problem-solving strategy.

  2. 2.

    Calibrated confidence quantification: The confidence estimates exhibit meaningful correlation with actual task success and solution reliability. In Case (A), confidence appropriately decreases upon error detection (95%→\rightarrow60%) and recovers after successful verification (60%→\rightarrow99%). In Case (B), consistently low confidence (5%–20%) throughout the trajectory reflects the agent’s awareness of inherent unreliability. In Case (C), the progressive confidence decline (90%→\rightarrow25%) demonstrates appropriate uncertainty revision as unexpected complexity is discovered during reasoning.
